Let
\[
x\ge y\ge z,\qquad x+y+z=1.
\]
By symmetry the integral is \(6\) times the integral over this chamber. Put
\[
y=ux,\qquad z=vy=uvx,\qquad 0\le u,v\le 1,
\]
so
\[
x=\frac1{1+u+uv},\quad y=\frac{u}{1+u+uv},\quad z=\frac{uv}{1+u+uv}.
\]
The Jacobian is
\[
dx\,dy=\frac{u}{(1+u+uv)^3}\,du\,dv.
\]
A direct substitution gives
\[
I_n=6\int_0^1\int_0^1
\frac{u(1-u)^2(1-v)^2(1-uv)^2}
{(1+u)(1+v)(1+uv)\sqrt v\,(1+u+uv)^{9/2}}
e^{-n u^2v/(1+u+uv)^3}\,du\,dv.
\]

Use the Mellin inversion formula
\[
e^{-t}=\frac1{2\pi i}\int \Gamma(s)t^{-s}\,ds.
\]
Then
\[
I_n=\frac1{2\pi i}\int \Gamma(s)n^{-s}L(s)\,ds,
\]
where
\[
L(s)=6\int_0^1\int_0^1
u^{1-2s}v^{-1/2-s}
\frac{(1-u)^2(1-v)^2(1-uv)^2(1+u+uv)^{3s-9/2}}
{(1+u)(1+v)(1+uv)}\,du\,dv.
\]
For large \(n\), we shift the contour right; the crossed poles of \(L(s)\) determine the asymptotics.

At \(s=\frac12\), the pole comes from \(v=0\). Its residue is
\[
-6\int_0^1\frac{(1-u)^2}{(1+u)^4}\,du=-1,
\]
so this contributes
\[
\sqrt\pi\,n^{-1/2}.
\]

At \(s=1\), the pole comes from \(u=0\). The analytic continuation gives
\[
6\int_0^1 v^{-3/2}\frac{(1-v)^2}{1+v}\,dv=-12\pi,
\]
hence the contribution is
\[
-6\pi n^{-1}.
\]

At \(s=\frac32\), there is a double pole. Expanding near \(u=v=0\),
\[
6\frac{(1-u)^2(1-v)^2(1-uv)^2}{(1+u)(1+v)(1+uv)}
=6-18u-18v+36uv+\cdots.
\]
Thus
\[
L(s)=\frac{18}{(s-\frac32)^2}-\frac{18}{s-\frac32}+O(1).
\]
Since
\[
\Gamma\!\left(\frac32\right)=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2},\qquad
\psi\!\left(\frac32\right)=2-\gamma-2\log 2,
\]
the \(s=\frac32\) contribution is
\[
n^{-3/2}\left(
9\sqrt\pi\log n
+9\sqrt\pi(\gamma+2\log2-1)
\right).
\]

Therefore
\[
I_n=
\sqrt\pi\,n^{-1/2}
-6\pi n^{-1}
+n^{-3/2}\left(
9\sqrt\pi\log n
+9\sqrt\pi(\gamma+2\log2-1)
\right)
+o(n^{-3/2}).
\]
Multiplying by \(n^{3/2}\) and subtracting the prescribed terms gives

\[
\boxed{9\sqrt{\pi}\,(\gamma+2\log 2-1)}.
\]
